blocks.prompt: The Bird That Laughs at Dawn
blocks.text: The kookaburra is a kingfisher. Most kingfishers dive into rivers and catch fish. The kookaburra does not. It sits on a branch and waits. It watches the ground with dark eyes. When it sees a beetle or a lizard, it drops down fast and grabs it. Then it flies back up to the branch. The kookaburra bangs its food on the wood before it eats. In the morning the whole family laughs together. The laugh is loud, and it goes a long way through the trees. It tells the other kookaburras that this tree is taken.

blocks.prompt: The Kingfisher That Will Not Fish
blocks.text: A kookaburra is a kingfisher, but it almost never fishes. Its cousins hover above rivers and plunge in headfirst after minnows. The kookaburra picks a branch instead, folds its wings, and waits. It can hold still for a long time, watching the grass below with dark eyes. When something moves, the bird drops like a stone, grabs it, and carries it back up to the branch. Then it does something surprising. It whacks its meal against the wood until the meal stops moving, and swallows it headfirst. A kookaburra will eat beetles, worms, mice, small birds, and even snakes. Its beak is long and heavy, more like a tool than a mouth. The laugh is not a joke either. A kookaburra family laughs together at first light and again at dusk, and the sound carries far through the trees. It means the same thing every time: this land is ours, go and find your own. Settlers in Australia called the bird the bushman's clock, because the laughing started right when it was time to get up.

blocks.prompt: Not a Fish in Sight
blocks.text: The laughing kookaburra belongs to the kingfisher family, which makes it an odd member of an odd club. Kingfishers are the small, bright birds that hang above a river, then fold and drop into the water after a minnow. The kookaburra is the heaviest kingfisher alive, close to a foot and a half long, with a beak like a pair of pliers. It hardly ever touches water. It hunts dry land instead. The method is patience. A kookaburra chooses a branch with a clear view of the grass, tucks its wings in, and becomes furniture. It can sit like that for many minutes, head still, eyes moving. When something below moves, a beetle or a worm or a mouse or a lizard, the bird drops without a sound, seizes it, and carries it back to the perch. Then it beats the animal against the wood until it stops struggling, and swallows it headfirst. A kookaburra will take a small snake this way. Its home is the strange part. A pair may nest in a hollow limb, or it may fly straight at a termite mound built in a tree, chip a tunnel into it, and let the termites seal the walls around the nest. The young that hatch there do not leave when they can fly. They stay for a year or more as helpers, carrying food to the next batch of chicks and joining the family chorus. That chorus is the laugh everyone knows. It is not amusement. A kookaburra family holds the same patch of forest all year, and rather than fight over the boundary every morning, they announce it. They gather, throw their heads back, and laugh, and the neighbors laugh back from their own trees. The sound carries much further than a kookaburra can chase an intruder, which is exactly the point.

blocks.prompt: A Laugh Is a Fence
blocks.text: The sound arrives before the light does. It starts low, a chuckle in the back of a throat, then gathers speed, climbs, and breaks into a cackle, and other birds fold in until the whole grove seems to be laughing at a joke nobody explained. The bird responsible is the laughing kookaburra, and the sound is not amusement. It is a boundary. Kookaburras are kingfishers, which is the first surprise. Their relatives are the small, hard, brilliant birds that hover over rivers and plunge in headfirst. The laughing kookaburra is the heaviest kingfisher on Earth, roughly a foot and a half long, carrying a beak that looks borrowed from a toolbox, and it hardly ever fishes. It hunts dry ground. A kookaburra selects a branch with a clean view and then does nothing at all, sometimes for many minutes, until something moves below. It drops silently, takes the animal, and returns to the perch, where it beats the meal against the wood until it goes limp and swallows it headfirst. Beetles, worms, mice, lizards, small birds, and snakes all end this way. The laughing is the more interesting weapon. A kookaburra family claims one patch of forest and stays in it all year. Instead of fighting over the boundary each morning, the group announces it. They gather, tilt their heads back, and chorus, and the neighbors chorus back from their own trees, and the map is redrawn without a feather lost. The call travels far beyond the distance the bird could ever chase an intruder, which is precisely why it works. Settlers called the kookaburra the bushman's clock, because the chorus arrived at first light whether anyone wanted it or not. The word family is meant literally. Kookaburras are cooperative breeders. A pair nests in a hollow limb, or flies at a termite mound built high in a tree, chips a tunnel into it, and lets the insects wall the chamber off around them. The young from earlier years do not go off to live alone. They stay on as helpers, carrying food to the new chicks, guarding the hollow, adding their voices to the dawn chorus. Very few birds keep a household this way. The name itself came from people who lived alongside the bird long before settlers did. It comes from guuguubarra, a Wiradjuri word that copies the call. The bird was named after its own sound, which may be the most honest naming any animal has received.

blocks.prompt: A Laugh That Is Not a Laugh
blocks.text: At dawn in an Australian forest a sound goes up that nobody forgets. It begins as a low chuckle, gathers speed, climbs into a cackle, and then several birds join at once until the whole grove seems to be laughing at a joke you were not told. The bird making it is the laughing kookaburra, and the sound is not amusement. It is a property line. Kookaburras are kingfishers, which is the first surprise. Their relatives are the small, brilliant birds that hover above rivers and plunge in headfirst after fish. The laughing kookaburra is the heaviest kingfisher on Earth, close to a foot and a half long, with a beak that looks borrowed from a toolbox, and it hardly ever fishes. It hunts dry land instead. The method is patience. A kookaburra selects a branch with a clear view, folds its wings, and becomes furniture. It can hold that pose for many minutes, eyes fixed on the grass. When something moves, a beetle, a worm, a mouse, a lizard, sometimes a snake, the bird drops without a sound, seizes it, and carries it back to the perch. Then comes the part children remember: it beats the animal against the wood until it stops struggling, and swallows it headfirst. The laughing is the more interesting weapon. A kookaburra family holds one patch of forest for the whole year and does not migrate away from it. Rather than fight over the boundary every morning, the group announces it. They gather, throw their heads back, and chorus, and the neighbors chorus back from their own trees, and the map is redrawn without a feather lost. The call travels much further than a kookaburra can chase an intruder, which is precisely the point. Early settlers called the bird the bushman's clock, because the chorus arrived at first light whether anyone wanted it or not. The word family is meant literally. Kookaburras are cooperative breeders. A pair nests in a hollow limb, or tunnels into a termite mound built high in a tree and lets the insects seal the walls around them, and the young from previous years do not leave. They stay on as helpers, feeding the new chicks, guarding the hollow, joining the chorus. Very few birds run a household this way. It is also not a gentle one. Kookaburra chicks hatch blind and naked with a sharp hook on the upper beak, and in the first days the older chicks sometimes turn that hook on the youngest. The hook falls away at about four weeks, long after it has done its work. The family that laughs together does not share equally. Humans have spread the sound around the world without meaning to. Settlers carried kookaburras west and south, and the birds now live in places they never evolved in, including Tasmania and a corner of New Zealand. Film carried the call further still. For decades, whenever a movie needed a jungle, a sound editor reached for the kookaburra, so audiences around the world learned to hear an Australian forest bird as the voice of rainforests it has never visited. That is the honest strangeness of the kookaburra. It is a kingfisher that avoids water, a bird whose laughter is a warning, a household that raises its young together and thins them at the same time, and a native of one continent standing in for the wild everywhere else. It is not laughing at us. We simply had no better word.
